paragraphs.heading: Reading life's family history
paragraphs.text: Phylogenetics studies how life has evolved over its history, working this out from features we can observe in organisms or in their genes. Researchers look at inherited traits such as DNA sequences, the amino acid sequences and shapes of proteins, and body form, and from these they infer how organisms are related. The result is a phylogenetic tree: a diagram of proposed relationships that reflects the inferred history. The tips of the tree stand for the things actually observed, which can be living groups or fossils.

paragraphs.heading: Rooted and unrooted trees
paragraphs.text: A tree can be drawn rooted or unrooted. A rooted tree marks the supposed common ancestor of all the groups it shows. An unrooted tree, also called a network, does not show that origin, and it makes no assumption about which way traits changed over time.

paragraphs.heading: Sorting and naming life
paragraphs.text: Phylogenetics is part of systematics, which uses the likenesses and differences between species to make sense of how they are related and where they came from. It is also used to map relationships among genes or single organisms, and it has become central to understanding biodiversity, evolution, ecology and genomes. Taxonomy, the naming and sorting of organisms, rests on the system Carolus Linnaeus built in the 1700s, which grouped species by their physical features. Today groupings are often based on DNA data, alone or together with body form.

paragraphs.heading: Uses in medicine
paragraphs.text: The same thinking helps in medicine. In cancer research, it can trace how groups of cells in a tumour change as the disease advances and during treatment. In drug discovery, it can point to species likely to share a medically useful trait with a known relative. Venoms from animals have given drugs such as ACE inhibitors and Prialt, and by screening close relatives of venomous species, biologists can pick out fish, snakes and lizards that may be venomous too.

paragraphs.heading: Uses in court
paragraphs.text: In forensic science, phylogenetic tools help judge DNA evidence, and they have been used in criminal trials both to clear people and to hold them responsible. In HIV cases, the method compares HIV genes to judge how closely two samples are related. But it cannot on its own prove that one person infected another, and it does not reveal which way the virus passed.

paragraphs.heading: From stories to statistics
paragraphs.text: Before 1950, ideas about how groups were related were usually told as narrative scenarios. These were often vague and gave no clear rules for weighing one hypothesis against another. Modern methods are computational, using approaches such as parsimony, maximum likelihood and Bayesian inference. Trees built from a larger total number of nucleotides, the units of a DNA sequence, are generally more accurate.
